big_picture: Nvidia’s CEO saga sparked massive stock moves and highlighted key-person risk, while separate reports flagged a US housing shortage driving fertility decline and soaring elder-care costs that strain families.

themes.title: Nvidia leadership turmoil drives market volatility
themes.explanation: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after an 11-day ouster (wsj-whats-news-b7ea90c22f, prof-g-markets-a6fe9a6e6f, marketplace-ffa33db71a), lifting the stock by more than 30% in a single day. The episode sparked a VIX spike to 40 and a correction in the S&P 500 (odd-lots-4375df19dc). Multiple investigations, including a DOJ probe into Megaspeed, underscore the regulatory backdrop (wsj-whats-news-27c6f62d3f).

themes.title: US housing shortage linked to record low fertility
themes.explanation: Freakonomics Radio reported the US fertility rate is at an all-time low of 1.6 children per woman, despite surveys showing a desire for larger families. Economists attribute the decline largely to a severe housing supply shortage that drives up costs and limits family formation.

themes.title: Elder-care costs outpace retirement savings
themes.explanation: WSJ Your Money Briefing highlighted that private nursing home rooms cost about $130,000 per year, while assisted-living facilities average $74,000 annually, far exceeding typical retirement savings and median incomes.

concept_of_the_day.explanation: Key-person risk arises when a company’s success and market valuation depend heavily on a single individual, often the founder or CEO. If that person leaves unexpectedly, the stock can tumble, as seen when Nvidia’s shares fell over 20% after Jensen Huang’s resignation and then surged 30%+ when the board reinstated him. The risk is amplified when the leader is tied to strategic assets like AI chips and faces regulatory scrutiny. Companies mitigate this by establishing clear succession plans and broader management teams.
